title: The ASCAP strike, Charlie Shavers and clean broadcasts
summary: On the ASCAP situation and her classical-jazzing, and Charlie Shavers quoting tunes in solos on the show.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: So in March of '42 -- and this must've been just before the recording ban went into effect, right? There was a twelve month or so or longer --
Yeah. What? Was that the ASCAP thing?
I thought it was the A.F. of M., but maybe I'm wrong about that. Maybe it was ASCAP.

Well, there was an ASCAP situation wherein the band -- the music couldn't be ASCAP music. And that Broadcast Music started publishing, because they had to start to writing a whole lot of brand new songs, you know. And there were a lot of popular songs that were ASCAP tunes that you could do. And then, of course --
Some people have suggested that the jazzing the classic thing was a result of that --
Well, I --
-- in 1942 (inaudible).
Well the thing about it is,

it made it that more prominent. It meant that they had to go out and dig up some more classics.
I recall --
But in your case, you've been doing that for five years.
Right.
I remembered during the ASCAP strike, we had the show, 'Flow Gently Sweet Rhythm.'
Yeah.
And, of course, Charlie Shavers had a tendency to improvise and use little passages from other songs.
And so they --
To quote in his solos.
Warned Charlie about this. He didn't care what he took off on. If he had, say, a fill-in, it might wound up to be 'Tea For Two,' or something like that.
So, in the studio, I imagine on the top floor where they monitoring the music, the guy up there was going crazy, because they never knew when Charlie was going to go into an ASCAP tune.

Yes, so, he had to keep it clean. But I remember I didn't get too involved -- I wasn't involved at all when they had the musicians strike, because I wasn't doing that much recording anyway. But I do remember that --
